attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his own post. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: "will never do" is a firm prediction with no hedge, so it is a scorable forecast with no deadline. The sentence also makes a present-tense claim ("cannot do"), which the proposition keeps.

contract.note: The contract tests the model itself and weight-level learning during deployment, not memory wrappers bolted on outside it. That is an ordinary reading of 'learn' as humans learn. But 'learn' and 're-evaluate' are undefined, so the reading decides what would count as an event.

evidence.note: SEAL abstract, June 2025. It describes standard LLMs as static, with no way to adapt their weights. Background only: it cannot settle a 'never' forecast.

SEAL v2, Sept 2025. A research prototype makes lasting self-directed weight updates, and its authors call it a 'promising step'. It was not deployed or independently reproduced, so it does not meet the early-refutation rule.

reviews.rationale: A 'never' forecast with no deadline cannot be confirmed. The only candidate refuting event (SEAL) is a lab prototype that has not been reproduced, so the early-refutation rule is not met. The packet shows no deployed LLM learning continually in its own weights by the cutoff, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words. The Woolf and Register quotes nearby are supporting material, not the claim itself.

semantics.note: This is a present-tense statement about agents. The proposition repeats his words literally, and the contract supplies the contextual meaning.

contract.note: In the same passage he cites 58% and 35% success rates and says agents are not autonomous, so taking 'at all' as hyperbole for 'not as dependable autonomous workers' is the ordinary reading. It does not stretch the claim either way. A literal zero-capability reading would give a different result.

evidence.note: CRMArena-Pro, May 2025, inside the target period. Leading agents managed about 35% success on multi-turn business tasks, failing most of them.
TheAgentCompany: the best agent completed 30% of tasks. The quoted abstract is v3 from Sept 2025, after the target period, so it counts only as context.
METR, March 2025. A 50% success rate on tasks of about 50 minutes shows real but unreliable capability. That fits the contextual reading and refutes only a literal zero-capability reading.

reviews.rationale: Read as the contract does (agents could not reliably and autonomously complete multi-step work), the claim matches the benchmark evidence from the period: about 35% multi-turn success on CRMArena-Pro, with METR showing only partial capability. Nothing in the packet shows agents reliably doing whole jobs.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words. The essays by others that he links are recommendations, not the claim.

semantics.note: This is a present-tense statement about what AI could do. The vibe-coding context (non-coders building working software) is kept in the contract.

contract.note: The contract reads the claim as AI being unable to reliably do software development by itself, not as AI being unable to write any code. That is the ordinary reading in context. The period just before the post is a reasonable choice, though the drafter picked it.

evidence.note: METR's GPT-5 report, Aug 7, 2025. It gives a 50% time horizon of about 2h17m, so the frontier model failed often on tasks of modest length.
Same report: an 80% time horizon of only about 25 minutes. Reliability falls away quickly beyond short tasks.

reviews.rationale: Independent METR measurements from the target period show frontier agents were unreliable at autonomous software tasks beyond short durations. That meets the support condition. The packet has no evidence of AI reliably building software end to end without human expertise.

semantics.note: The sentence bundles value judgments ('good', 'death of the art of technology', 'by design') into one polemical line. It is rhetoric or normative, not a testable observation.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to invent measures, comparators or a harmed party that the speaker did not supply. Any test would depend on choices the evaluator made up.

reviews.rationale: This is a compound rhetorical value judgment with no measure, no period and no named party. 'Financially ruinous' has no stated victim, and 'cognitive load' has no baseline. There is nothing fair to score it against, so it is not adjudicable. The case is not broken.
